Problem 1 - Tidyverse: New Zealand

From ?nzge, each row is the number of votes for one party (or the informal votes) at one voting place, for one vote type (Candidate = electorate vote, Party = list vote), in one election year. Because the two vote types are cast on the same ballot, they are always summarised separately below.

a. Vote count per year and vote type

Code 
nzge |>
  group_by(election_year, voting_type) |>
  summarise(total_votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total_votes)) |>
  mutate(election_year = as.character(election_year)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Year", "Vote type", "Total votes"),
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

c. Winning party by year and vote type

Code 
nzge |>
  filter(!str_detect(party, "^Informal")) |>
  group_by(election_year, voting_type, party) |>
  summarise(votes = sum(votes), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  slice_max(votes, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(election_year, voting_type, party) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = voting_type, values_from = party) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Year", "Candidate vote winner", "Party vote winner"))
Year Candidate vote winner Party vote winner
2002 Labour Party Labour Party
2005 National Party Labour Party
2008 National Party National Party
2011 National Party National Party
2014 National Party National Party
2017 National Party National Party

Labour won both votes in 2002. In 2005 the votes split: National narrowly won the Candidate vote (by about 800 votes nationally) while Labour won the Party vote, which is what determines seat allocation under MMP. From 2008 to 2017 the National Party won both votes.

tourney_level codes are A (ATP 250/500), M (Masters 1000), G (Grand Slams), F (season finals) and D (Davis Cup). Every Davis Cup tie (one country vs. another) gets its own tourney_id, so the 60 Davis Cup IDs are rubbers of a single team competition, not separate tournaments. The Laver Cup is also a team exhibition and has no final.

a. Number of tournaments in 2019

Code 
atp |>
  summarise(
    all_tourney_ids         = n_distinct(tourney_id),
    davis_cup_ties          = n_distinct(tourney_id[tourney_level == "D"]),
    individual_tournaments  = n_distinct(tourney_id[tourney_level != "D" &
                                                    tourney_name != "Laver Cup"])
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("All tourney IDs", "Davis Cup ties",
                      "Individual tournaments"))
All tourney IDs Davis Cup ties Individual tournaments
128 60 67

There are 128 distinct tourney_ids, but 60 are Davis Cup ties and one is the Laver Cup. Counting individual tournaments that crown a champion, 67 tournaments took place in 2019 (68 if the Laver Cup is counted as one event, 69 if the Davis Cup is also counted as a single tournament).

c. Do winners hit more aces than losers?

Each match gives a natural pair (winner’s aces, loser’s aces), so a paired t-test on the per-match difference is appropriate. The test is computed by hand inside a dplyr pipeline.

Code 
atp |>
  filter(!is.na(w_ace), !is.na(l_ace)) |>
  mutate(ace_diff = w_ace - l_ace) |>
  summarise(
    n_matches       = n(),
    mean_w_ace      = mean(w_ace),
    mean_l_ace      = mean(l_ace),
    mean_diff       = mean(ace_diff),
    se_diff         = sd(ace_diff) / sqrt(n_matches),
    t_stat          = mean_diff / se_diff,
    p_value_one_sid = pt(t_stat, df = n_matches - 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 4)
n_matches mean_w_ace mean_l_ace mean_diff se_diff t_stat p_value_one_sid
2694 7.4974 5.7925 1.7049 0.1378 12.373 0

Over the 2,694 matches with ace data, winners averaged 7.5 aces and losers 5.8, a mean difference of about 1.7 aces per match. The one-sided paired test (H0: mean difference = 0, H1: winners hit more aces) gives t = 12.4 on 2,693 degrees of freedom and a p-value of about 1.5e-34, so there is strong evidence that match winners hit more aces than losers. (This is an association; serving well both produces aces and wins matches.)

d. Highest win rate (at least 5 matches)

Code 
atp |>
  select(winner_name, loser_name) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "result", values_to = "player") |>
  group_by(player) |>
  summarise(matches  = n(),
            wins     = sum(result == "winner_name"),
            win_rate = wins / matches,
            .groups  = "drop") |>
  filter(matches >= 5) |>
  slice_max(win_rate, n = 5) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Player", "Matches", "Wins", "Win rate"), digits = 3)
Player Matches Wins Win rate
Rafael Nadal 69 60 0.870
Novak Djokovic 69 58 0.841
Roger Federer 66 55 0.833
Daniil Medvedev 80 59 0.738
Kevin Anderson 15 11 0.733

Among players with at least 5 matches, Rafael Nadal has the highest win rate: 60 wins in 69 matches (87.0%), ahead of Djokovic (84.1%) and Federer (83.3%). All matches in the file are counted, including Davis Cup rubbers and walkovers.

Problem 3 - Visualization

Code 
covid_url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nytimes/covid-19-data/",
                    "refs/heads/master/rolling-averages/us-states.csv")
territories <- c("Puerto Rico", "Guam", "Virgin Islands",
                 "Northern Mariana Islands", "American Samoa")
covid <- read_csv(covid_url, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!state %in% territories)   # 50 states + DC
range(covid$date)
[1] "2020-01-21" "2023-03-23"

cases_avg is the 7-day rolling average of new cases and cases_avg_per_100k is the same quantity per 100,000 residents, so it is already adjusted for population.

a. Major and minor spikes

Code 
national <- covid |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(cases_avg = sum(cases_avg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# label the highest point inside each wave's window
waves <- tribble(
  ~wave,                   ~start,       ~end,         ~type,
  "Spring 2020",           "2020-03-01", "2020-05-31", "Minor",
  "Summer 2020",           "2020-06-01", "2020-09-15", "Minor",
  "Winter 2020-21",        "2020-10-01", "2021-03-01", "Major",
  "Spring 2021",           "2021-03-01", "2021-06-01", "Minor",
  "Delta (2021)",          "2021-07-01", "2021-11-01", "Major",
  "Omicron (2022)",        "2021-12-01", "2022-03-01", "Major",
  "Summer 2022 (BA.5)",    "2022-05-01", "2022-09-30", "Minor",
  "Winter 2022-23",        "2022-11-01", "2023-02-01", "Minor"
) |>
  mutate(across(c(start, end), as.Date))

peaks <- waves |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(peak = list(national |>
                       filter(date >= start, date < end) |>
                       slice_max(cases_avg, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  unnest(peak)

ggplot(national, aes(date, cases_avg / 1000)) +
  geom_area(fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 150, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = peaks, aes(colour = type), size = 2.5) +
  geom_text_repel(data = peaks,
                  aes(label = paste0(wave, "\n",
                                     scales::comma(round(cases_avg / 1000)),
                                     "k/day"),
                      colour = type),
                  size = 3.2, nudge_y = 60, segment.colour = "grey60",
                  lineheight = 0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2022-10-01"), y = 175,
           label = "Major threshold: 150k/day", hjust = 0, size = 3,
           colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Major = "#B2182B", Minor = "#2166AC"),
                      name = "Spike") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y",
               expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "k"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(title = "U.S. daily new COVID-19 cases: three major and five minor waves",
       subtitle = "7-day average of reported new cases, 50 states + DC",
       x = NULL, y = "New cases per day (thousands)",
       caption = "Source: The New York Times, COVID-19 data (rolling averages)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

I count 8 spikes: 3 major and 5 minor. I define a major spike as a wave whose national 7-day average exceeded 150,000 cases/day (dashed line): winter 2020-21, the Delta wave (late summer 2021), and the Omicron wave (January 2022, peaking around 800k/day, more than three times any other wave). The minor spikes are spring 2020, summer 2020, spring 2021, summer 2022 (BA.5) and winter 2022-23. Waves after early 2022 are likely understated because home testing meant many cases were never reported.

b. Highest vs. lowest overall rates

The overall rate per population is the total reported cases per 100,000 residents. Summing the daily 7-day average per 100k over the whole period gives that cumulative rate.

Code 
state_rates <- covid |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(total_per_100k = sum(cases_avg_per_100k, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total_per_100k))

extremes <- bind_rows(
  slice_head(state_rates, n = 5) |> mutate(group = "Highest 5 states"),
  slice_tail(state_rates, n = 5) |> mutate(group = "Lowest 5 states")
)
extremes |>
  kable(col.names = c("State", "Total cases per 100k", "Group"),
        digits = 0, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
State Total cases per 100k Group
Rhode Island 43,296 Highest 5 states
Alaska 41,835 Highest 5 states
Kentucky 39,042 Highest 5 states
North Dakota 37,604 Highest 5 states
Tennessee 36,181 Highest 5 states
District of Columbia 25,344 Lowest 5 states
Vermont 24,518 Lowest 5 states
Oregon 22,915 Lowest 5 states
Maryland 22,091 Lowest 5 states
Maine 22,020 Lowest 5 states
Code 
cum <- covid |>
  arrange(state, date) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  mutate(cum_per_100k = cumsum(replace_na(cases_avg_per_100k, 0))) |>
  ungroup()

cum_ext <- cum |>
  inner_join(extremes |> select(state, group), by = "state")

end_labels <- cum_ext |>
  filter(date == max(date))

ggplot(cum, aes(date, cum_per_100k / 1000, group = state)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = cum_ext, aes(colour = group), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(data = end_labels,
                  aes(label = state, colour = group),
                  direction = "y", hjust = 0, nudge_x = 25, size = 3.2,
                  segment.colour = "grey70", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Highest 5 states" = "#B2182B",
                                 "Lowest 5 states" = "#2166AC"),
                      name = NULL) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y",
               expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.15))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "k")) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents",
       subtitle = paste("Five states with the highest and lowest totals;",
                        "grey lines are all other states and DC"),
       x = NULL, y = "Cumulative cases per 100k (thousands)",
       caption = "Source: The New York Times, COVID-19 data (rolling averages)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
Code 
covid |>
  inner_join(extremes |> select(state, group), by = "state") |>
  mutate(state = factor(state, levels = extremes$state)) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, cases_avg_per_100k, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ state, nrow = 2) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Highest 5 states" = "#B2182B",
                                 "Lowest 5 states" = "#2166AC")) +
  labs(title = "Daily new COVID-19 cases per 100,000 residents",
       subtitle = paste("7-day average. Top row (red): five highest-total states;",
                        "bottom row (blue): five lowest"),
       x = NULL, y = "New cases per 100k per day",
       caption = "Source: The New York Times, COVID-19 data (rolling averages)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

The highest-rate states are Rhode Island, Alaska, Kentucky, North Dakota and Tennessee; the lowest are Maine, Maryland, Oregon, Vermont and DC.

  • Spring 2020: the ordering was nearly reversed. DC, Rhode Island and Maryland had the earliest outbreaks, while Alaska, Oregon and Vermont had almost no cases.
  • Fall/winter 2020-21: this is where the groups split. North Dakota, Tennessee, Kentucky and Rhode Island had very large surges (North Dakota reached about 12,900 cumulative cases per 100k by March 2021), while Vermont, Maine and Oregon stayed below about 3,700.
  • Delta (summer-fall 2021): the gap widened again. Alaska, Kentucky, Tennessee and North Dakota added roughly 6,000 to 11,000 cases per 100k between July and December 2021, versus roughly 2,000 to 4,000 in the low-rate states.
  • Omicron (winter 2021-22): every state spiked at about the same time, and the increase was similar in both groups (Rhode Island had the tallest peak, about 500 daily cases per 100k). After March 2022 the curves rise at similar slopes.

So the difference between the groups was built up mostly in the 2020-21 winter and Delta waves, not in Omicron, when the whole country was hit at once.

c. First five states to experience COVID-19 substantially

I define “substantial” as the 7-day average first reaching 5 new cases per 100,000 residents per day, which puts states of different sizes on the same footing.

Code 
threshold <- 5

first_dates <- covid |>
  filter(cases_avg_per_100k >= threshold) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(first_date = min(date), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(first_date)

first_five <- first_dates |> slice_head(n = 5)
first_five |>
  kable(col.names = c("State", paste("First day with >=", threshold,
                                     "cases per 100k")))
State First day with >= 5 cases per 100k
New York 2020-03-21
New Jersey 2020-03-24
Louisiana 2020-03-26
Massachusetts 2020-03-27
Connecticut 2020-03-28
Code 
early <- covid |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2020-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2020-04-15"),
         cases_avg_per_100k > 0) |>   # log scale cannot show zeros
  mutate(highlight = if_else(state %in% first_five$state, state, "Other"))

ggplot(early, aes(date, cases_avg_per_100k, group = state)) +
  geom_line(data = filter(early, highlight == "Other"),
            colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = filter(early, highlight != "Other"),
            aes(colour = highlight), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = threshold, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = first_five |>
               left_join(covid, by = c("state", "first_date" = "date")),
             aes(first_date, cases_avg_per_100k, colour = state),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.5) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2020-03-02"), y = threshold * 1.15,
           label = "5 cases per 100k", hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100),
                labels = c("0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = "First five states",
                      breaks = first_five$state) +
  labs(title = "Early spread: the first five states to reach 5 daily cases per 100k",
       subtitle = "7-day average of new cases per 100,000 residents, March 1 - April 15, 2020 (log scale)",
       x = NULL, y = "New cases per 100k per day (log scale)",
       caption = "Points mark the first day each highlighted state crossed the threshold.\nSource: The New York Times, COVID-19 data (rolling averages)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

By this measure the first five states were New York, New Jersey, Louisiana, Massachusetts and Connecticut, all crossing the threshold between March 21 and March 28, 2020. The answer is fairly robust: with a 10 per 100k threshold the same states plus Michigan lead the list, though at a looser 1 per 100k threshold Washington (the first reported U.S. case, January 2020) moves to the front.
